MetroGrid

Every metro train has an air compressor that powers its brakes and doors. Metro Grid watches each one and warns the depot when it starts behaving differently from its healthy self.

    The model

    The model is an autoencoder: a small neural network that squeezes 14 measurements through a narrow middle layer and tries to rebuild them. We trained it only on minutes when Train A's compressor was healthy, so it gets very good at rebuilding healthy behaviour and bad at anything else. When a compressor starts to leak, the rebuild gets worse. That error, smoothed over an hour, becomes the health index, and a long stretch of high error becomes an alarm.

    Does the browser match the notebook?

    The model runs inside this page. To show it is the same model as in our report, every minute was scored twice, once in the Colab notebook and once here, and the answers are compared below.

    What the model looks at

    Fourteen measurements worked out from the raw sensors every minute. Each one was picked because an air or oil leak changes it.

      Demo moments

      Leak injection test · Train A

      How the test works: we took 12 real days when Train A was healthy and edited each recording to look as if a leak had started. With a leak, air escapes, so while the compressor rests the pressure falls faster, and when it pumps it takes longer to fill back up. We squeezed and stretched the real resting and pumping stretches to match, growing the leak over 12 hours and then holding it for 12 more. The slider sets the leak size, and the bars show how often each model raised an alarm. 0× adds no leak, which checks that the editing alone doesn't cause false alarms. This was only for testing; no model was trained on it.
